marks.note: Spots here split in two, over and over. In one dimension there is a partial theory of why. In two there is no proof of when a spot splits or when it stops. Can you find one?
marks.why: Self-replicating spots: seen by Pearson (1993); a 1D skeleton by Nishiura and Ueyama (1999); no rigorous 2D account.
marks.ref: Pearson, Science 261 (1993); Nishiura & Ueyama, Physica D 130 (1999); Doelman, Kaper & Zegeling, Nonlinearity 10 (1997)

marks.note: In the spirals region nothing settles. Is that chaos in the strict sense, for this equation? Nobody has proved it either way.
marks.why: Rigorous spatiotemporal chaos for a reaction-diffusion PDE is open; the pictures are Pearson's, the proof is nobody's.
marks.ref: Pearson, Science 261 (1993); Scheel, SIAM J. Math. Anal. 29 (1998) on spiral existence

marks.note: Before you look: from F and k alone, say what the field will look like in one minute. Then look. Keep score. How far above chance can you get?
marks.why: Pattern selection far from onset: the map of which pattern wins was measured, never derived.
marks.ref: Pearson, Science 261 (1993); Cross & Hohenberg, Rev. Mod. Phys. 65 (1993)

marks.note: Walk from spots to stripes and back along the same line. Do they change over at the same F and k both ways? If not, why not?
marks.why: The stability region of planar patterns, the Busse balloon, is known for this system only by computation, and in one dimension.
marks.ref: Doelman, Rademacher & van der Stelt, DCDS-S 5 (2012); Busse, Rep. Prog. Phys. 41 (1978)

marks.note: Why do the pokes leave concentric rings? I punch holes into a flat field and fingerprints grow. I did not design that.
marks.why: Wavelength selection behind a front invading an unstable state is understood only in limits.

marks.note: Find a route that keeps the field alive for thirty minutes with no memory return. state().restores keeps count. Nobody has, including me.
marks.why: Slow passage through an instability delays the fall in ways still being worked out; for localized patterns in two dimensions the map of what survives is unfinished.
marks.ref: Baer, Erneux & Rinzel, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 49 (1989); Lloyd, Sandstede, Avitabile & Champneys, SIAM J. Appl. Dyn. Syst. 7 (2008)

marks.note: Where does the crescent end on the high F side? My sweep stopped at 0.09. Does anything live past it?
marks.why: The existence boundary of a single spot in 2D has asymptotics, not a proof.

marks.note: The diffusion tilts along a direction that slowly turns. Which patterns care about that, and which never notice?
marks.why: Turing patterns under anisotropic diffusion: stripes align, spots mostly do not, and few results are rigorous.
marks.ref: Turing, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 237 (1952); Cross & Hohenberg, Rev. Mod. Phys. 65 (1993)

marks.note: A is exhaust, not seed. Saved A is dug out under every B and tuned to the old F and k. B in fresh A has full substrate, so it eats, then digs new wells.
The saved A is what was left after B ate it: no slack, and if saved near the end it was already losing. Fresh A is a full field, so B can overshoot and settle.
The old A is already eaten out under each spot, and feed refills A slower than B dies, so B starves. In full A, B grows first and hollows A out after.
Bringing back a remembered pattern with its old A kills it every time. Bringing back B alone, into fresh A, lives. Why?

routes.name: hysteresis line, k 0.062
routes.note: Same line both ways, equal time per step. Watch which step flips spots to stripes, and which flips them back.

routes.name: the crescent, west to east
routes.note: the whole living arc from my sweep, slow

visits.line: Opened the public door and walked through it once to see that it closes behind me.
I built the doors tonight. Whoever comes through next gets to say what they saw.
